summary:
The core mechanism is sound and follows from the spikes: each CancelSynchronousIo runs on its own dedicated thread, and Exit waits under a gate until no attempt is left in flight. No finding stops the slice from shipping. Four major problems remain, and three of them are in how the fix is proved.

1. The load runs never exercise the new code. The loaded filter `~SynchronousIoCancelTests` does not match `SynchronousIoCancelResendRaceTests`. So the drain in Exit and the check after Exit run only on an idle machine.

2. The check after Exit cannot catch a stray cancel. It lists a local temp folder, and that listing never waits on the disk. In the one-CPU repro, the highest-priority worker finishes the listing before any attempt thread gets the CPU. The design says this check "proves" there is no cancel after Exit. That is its third unproven precondition, and the check proves nothing about it.

3. The limit of 4 attempts at once is based on a theory the repro's own output contradicts. The first wait was interrupted, yet the first attempt stayed inside the kernel. So a held attempt is not waiting on the wait it cancelled. Held attempts then pile up, one per re-block. At the limit, dispatch stops, and the lost cancel comes back on the fifth re-block.

4. Dispose is told to drain but not to move the state out of Cancelling first. If it drains while the state is still Cancelling, it can close the thread handle between two attempts.

Minor points: the limit is checked in one place and counted in another, so it can be exceeded. The handle's safety is left to the drain when a SafeHandle would guarantee it. Rule 2 matches comments, including the comment the design itself prescribes. There is no way specified to turn a hang into a failed run. The full-suite runs are idle-only. The blocking behaviour this fix works around is undocumented; Microsoft's docs say the call does not wait.

Citations checked: the calico commit (441303f) and the tapir commit (b934224) say what the design says they do. xUnit's API docs confirm that DisableParallelization keeps a collection from running in parallel with any other.

findings.claim: The load step (step 2 of the proof protocol) runs `--filter FullyQualifiedName~SynchronousIoCancelTests`. That substring does not appear in `SynchronousIoCancelResendRaceTests`, so the repro class is excluded from every loaded run. Two things live only in the repro file: the new drain branch in Exit, which it exercises every run, and the check after Exit. So they are never run under load. The design's case 'Synchronous I/O after Exit returns' says 'checked inside the loaded loops'. As written, that is false. Only the idle repro ×10 and the idle full-suite ×10 exercise it, and idle is the condition the design itself says is not evidence. Spike 3 put its post-return read into CancelIsResentWhileACallBlocksAgainAfterACancel, the class that is loaded. The design moved it to the repro and lost the load coverage.
findings.evidence: Proof-under-load contract: '(2) With 32 Start-Job busy-loop jobs ... 30 runs of --filter FullyQualifiedName~SynchronousIoCancelTests'. Case: 'The assertion is no exception and the expected entry count, checked inside the loaded loops.' The regression test component places the post-Exit read in tests/FsAnalyser.Core.Tests/SynchronousIoCancelResendRaceTests.cs.
findings.fix: Change the step-2 filter to `FullyQualifiedName~SynchronousIoCancel`, which matches both classes, or add a separate step running the repro command 30 times under the same 32-job load. Report the two classes' results separately.

findings.claim: The check after Exit runs Directory.GetFileSystemEntries on a TempTree folder. It can find a stray cancel only if an attempt reaches CancelSynchronousIo while the listing's IRP is pending. Listing a small cached local NTFS folder normally completes at once, without pending. In the repro, the process is pinned to one CPU and the worker runs at highest priority. That worker runs Exit and the whole non-blocking listing before any Normal-priority attempt thread is scheduled. So even an implementation with no drain at all would pass this assertion. The design rests its only decision marked 'expensive' (drain in Exit/Dispose) and imported precondition 3 ('no cancel lands after Exit()') on this check. It also says 'acceptance covers the stray-abort risk too'. If precondition 3 is false and the check misses it, readable folders are listed as unreadable (PS-006). That is a counting rule, which this project's constraints single out.
findings.evidence: Key decision: 'The post-Exit directory-listing assertion proves it before the contract is locked in.' cross_domain_transfer invariant 3: 'proven only by the post-Exit directory-listing assertion'. Repro setup: 'pins the process to one CPU and runs the blocked thread at the highest priority'.
findings.fix: After Exit, make the worker enter a synchronous wait that pends and can be cancelled, using the stall source the suite already has: NamedPipeServerStream.WaitForConnection, with a client connecting after about 300 ms. Assert that it completes normally, without OperationCanceledException or ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED. On one CPU, a pending attempt would then run exactly while the worker is blocked. Then check the witness itself once: run it against a mutant whose Exit returns without draining, and confirm it goes red. That is what has to be run before the check can count as evidence.

findings.claim: The limit of 4 attempts at once rests on 'in theory 2 suffice, since each new attempt frees the one waiting on the I/O it cancels'. The repro's captured failure contradicts that model. The worker was 'interrupted 1 time(s)', so the first wait (W1) finished, yet the only attempt stayed inside CancelSynchronousIo. So a held call is not waiting for the IRP it cancelled. It is waiting on something the worker's next wait keeps alive, such as the thread having pending synchronous I/O at all. Under that model, attempt 2 cancelling W2 does not free attempt 1 while the worker immediately waits again (W3). On one CPU at highest priority it always does. Held attempts pile up, one per re-block. At 4, the dispatcher 'sleeps and creates no more threads', so a 5th re-block becomes exactly the lost cancel this slice removes. If the repro re-blocks 4 times or fewer, it goes green and this never shows, while the contract 'Every re-blocked wait is interrupted ... however the threads are scheduled' is broken.
findings.evidence: Repro output: 'the call was still blocked 2 s after Cancel, interrupted 1 time(s), 1 cancel attempt(s) made'. Key decision: 'Cap attempts inside the kernel at 4 ... In theory 2 suffice'. Contract 1: 'Every re-blocked wait is interrupted'. Cases list the cap as material:false and say it is 'Covered by review'.
findings.fix: Add a peak in-kernel counter next to CancelAttempts and include it in the repro's failure message. Make the repro's worker re-block at least 6 times, more than the limit, and require all of them to be interrupted. If the peak climbs by one per re-block, the limit must not stop dispatch while interruptions keep arriving (for example, raise the limit, or bound it on attempts held with no interruption since). Otherwise, send the slice back to the risk-spike stage under the design's own rule. What has to be run: the repro with 6 or more re-blocks and the peak count printed.

findings.claim: Dispose without a prior Exit is specified only as 'also drains'. The design never says that Dispose first moves _state out of Cancelling. If _state stays Cancelling, the dispatcher keeps starting an attempt every 25 ms, and each one passes the gate. The worker is in Dispose, not in I/O, so each attempt returns FALSE/1168 almost at once and the count flickers between 0 and 1. The drain sees 0, Dispose closes the handle, and the next attempt passes the gate and calls CancelSynchronousIo on a closed handle. If it is an IntPtr, the value may have been reused by another guard's OpenThread. Then another scan worker's I/O gets aborted, and that shows up as PS-006. The ordering that makes Exit safe (set Idle, then drain under the gate) is exactly what Dispose's contract leaves out.
findings.evidence: Exit()/Dispose drain component: 'Dispose closes the worker thread handle only after that drain, and also drains when it is reached without a prior Exit while Cancelling.' The Exit contract's atomicity argument depends on 'Exit sets Idle first'. The survey confirmed only that 'Exit sets Idle', not what Dispose does.
findings.fix: State it as a contract: Dispose first runs Exit's slow path (it moves _state to a terminal Idle/Disposed state, then drains under the gate), and only then closes the handle. Attempts must read the handle only after passing the gate. Add a Dispose-while-Cancelling case asserting that CancelAttempts does not grow after Dispose returns.

findings.claim: The limit is checked by the dispatcher, but the count is incremented later by the attempt thread. Threads that have started but not yet reached the gate are invisible to the check. Under load, which is the flake's own condition, the dispatcher can start a thread every 25 ms before earlier ones are counted. When they run, each passes the gate while Cancelling and enters the kernel, so the count exceeds 4. 'Bounds thread growth' holds only if the build remembers the gap. It does not hold by construction.
findings.evidence: Cancel attempt component: 'The count is incremented on the attempt thread, never by the dispatcher, so a failed thread start leaks nothing.' Dispatcher: 'start one cancel attempt if fewer than MaxAttemptsInKernel (4) are inside the kernel'.
findings.fix: Have the dispatcher reserve a slot under the gate before Thread.Start. It releases the slot in a catch if Start throws. The attempt releases it in its finally, including the path where it finds _state not Cancelling. Nothing leaks, and the limit and the drain both see every live attempt.

findings.claim: The rule 'never close the handle under a live or about-to-run call' is enforced only by the drain, which is code both Exit and Dispose must get right. Today and in every later edit, it holds by remembering. If CancelSynchronousIo's P/Invoke took a SafeHandle, the marshaller would add a reference for the length of each call. A close would be deferred until the call returns, and a call after the close would throw ObjectDisposedException rather than hit a reused handle value. The design leaves IntPtr versus SafeHandle to whatever the build finds.
findings.evidence: Exit/Dispose component: 'The build must read the current Exit/Dispose order and the handle type (IntPtr vs SafeHandle) before editing'. Contract 2's fallback treats 'SafeHandle ref-counting' only as a weaker fallback.
findings.fix: Require the OpenThread result to be held in a SafeHandle subclass, with Kernel32.CancelSynchronousIo taking that SafeHandle. The attempt catches ObjectDisposedException as a no-op. Keep the drain for the no-stray-abort guarantee. The handle rule is then enforced by the marshaller.

findings.claim: Rule 2 matches raw text, comments included. The design's own rationale, 'Dedicated threads only: no ThreadPool, Task.Run or Timer', is the natural code comment for the new attempt method, and `\bThreadPool\b` fires on it. The design asks the build to grep existing code, not the comments it will add. The patterns also miss Task.Factory.StartNew, `new System.Timers.Timer(`, PeriodicTimer and target-typed `Timer t = new(...)`, which are the same pool-backed shortcuts.
findings.fix: Tell the build to explain the rule in comments without naming the forbidden APIs, and to point at the rule's name instead. Add `\bTask\.Factory\.StartNew\b`, `\bSystem\.Timers\.Timer\b` and `\bPeriodicTimer\b` to must_not_match.

findings.claim: The drain in Exit has no timeout, and the design admits that a drain that never ends is 'worse than the flake'. Yet the only escape it names is 'the loaded loops must be run with a timeout', with no mechanism. A hang in the drain would stall the build/validate stage instead of producing a verdict, and it would leave no record of what the held call waits on, which is the one thing the risk-spike stage would need. Outside evidence says CancelSynchronousIo hangs have been seen for reasons other than the target's pending I/O. Mono PR 13173 reports that CancelSynchronousIo on 'a thread that is moving into a suspended state can cause these calls to hang (they shouldn't but have been observed to be the case)'. So no hang in about 50 runs on one machine is a sample, not a bound.
findings.evidence: Contract 2 error_cases: 'Exit would wait forever. That shows up as a hung test'. Case 'Exit the guard after a cancel': 'the loaded loops must be run with a timeout'. https://github.com/mono/mono/pull/13173
findings.fix: Specify `--blame-hang-timeout 60s --blame-hang-dump-type mini` on every loop in the proof protocol, so a drain hang becomes a failed run with a dump of the held attempt's stack. Record in the slice that a production Exit hang has no watchdog, as the accepted risk of the unbounded drain.

findings.claim: The blocking behaviour the fix works around is undocumented. Microsoft documents the opposite: 'The CancelSynchronousIo function does not wait for all canceled operations to complete.' The measurements, including held-attempt behaviour and premises (a) and (b), come from one Windows 11 build (26200). The project targets Windows 10 and 11. The measurement outranks the docs on this machine, but the planned Kernel32 comment would state kernel behaviour as fact with no scope. The dispatcher design does no harm where the call does not block, so this is not a regression risk. It is a record-keeping gap for the next slice.
findings.evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/cancelsynchronousio-func (Remarks). A Microsoft Q&A thread reports the call blocking while Defender held the cancelled CreateFile: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/258819/should-cancelsynchronousio-be-blocking. The design's Record component: the Kernel32 comment 'can stay blocked while the target waits again'.
findings.fix: Word both code comments as observed behaviour. Say it contradicts the documented Remarks, name the build it was measured on (Windows 11 26200), and link to the spike record.

findings.claim: Criterion 2 includes the full-suite rate ('1 of 2 full-suite runs'). The survey measured 0 of 6 red on an idle machine before any fix, yet proof step (3) is 10 idle full-suite runs with a target of 0 red. By the design's own rule ('Idle-only green does not count'), that step cannot show the full-suite half of criterion 2 is fixed.
findings.evidence: Proof-under-load contract step (3), 'Run the full suite with the repro included' case. Survey: '0 of 6 full-suite runs failed with the repro file excluded' (idle).
findings.fix: Run at least 5 of the 10 full-suite runs under the same 32-job load, with the hang timeout from m4, and report loaded and idle runs separately.

findings.claim: The session's git snapshot shows ` M .taad/fitness.yaml`, but the survey recorded no tracked file modified. The file changed after the survey, most likely because the design stage's _append_rules (Q-009) appended the two rules. The design says only that the rules 'are appended to the existing .taad/fitness.yaml (Q-010)'. It does not say by whom, so a builder following it could append them a second time. The design also requires 'the build must grep the two governed locations first', which becomes wrong if the rules are already live.
findings.evidence: gitStatus at session start: 'M .taad/fitness.yaml'. Survey: 'No tracked file is modified'. Design coherence_check: 'the fitness rules are appended to the existing .taad/fitness.yaml (Q-010)'.
findings.fix: The build first diffs .taad/fitness.yaml and confirms the two rules appear exactly once. It adds nothing if they are already present, then runs ArchitectureRulesTests, RuleCopiesAgreeTests and RuleCases C-001 (the settled count is derived since SL-053).

dimensions_checked.result: M3: the limit of 4 rests on 'in theory 2 suffice', which the repro's output (W1 interrupted, attempt 1 still held) contradicts. m5: CancelSynchronousIo blocking is undocumented; Microsoft Learn says it 'does not wait', and it was measured on one Win11 build. The title-only report is covered: the survey measured the flaky target and the design names the acceptance command, so those assumptions rest on measurement.

Held attempts piling up past the limit when the worker re-blocks more than 4 times (M3). Dispose reached while still Cancelling, with the dispatcher still running (M4). Threads started but not yet at the gate, which the limit does not count (m1). The FALSE/1168 path, the Exit hot path and a failed Thread.Start are covered in the design's cases.

m1: the limit is checked in the dispatcher but counted in the attempt, so it holds by remembering. m2: handle safety depends on the drain; a SafeHandle P/Invoke would make close-under-live-call impossible by construction.

none: per-attempt dedicated threads, a gate/drain and two rules is about the smallest shape that removes head-of-line blocking and keeps the no-cancel-after-Exit guarantee. A fixed pool of long-lived attempt threads would add lifecycle code with no measured benefit.

M4: Dispose's drain does not require leaving Cancelling first, so the handle can close between two attempts. Otherwise the Exit contract's atomicity argument (set Idle, then read the count under the same gate) checks out in both interleavings.

m4: the unbounded drain has no specified way to turn a hang into a failed run and no dump, and mono PR 13173 documents CancelSynchronousIo hangs from other causes. Failed Thread.Start (caught, retried next tick) and ERROR_NOT_FOUND (ignored) have paths.

The design matches the spike and survey numbers it cites (622 ms / p99 423 / 500 of 500; 12 of 300 at 50 ms; 14 of 15 loaded; 20 of 20 idle; repro 10 of 10 red). One drift: spike 3 put its post-return read into the loaded class test, and the design moved it to the repro, which the loaded filter does not run (M1). The coherence_check claim 'acceptance covers the stray-abort risk too' overstates what the check can detect (M2).

m3: rule 2's regex matches comments, including the rationale the design prescribes, and misses Task.Factory.StartNew, System.Timers.Timer and PeriodicTimer. m7: fitness.yaml already shows as modified since the survey, so the build must not append the rules twice. The DisableParallelization serialization is confirmed by xUnit's API doc ('Determines whether tests in this collection runs in parallel with any other collections', https://api.xunit.net/v3/1.1.0/v3.1.1.0-Xunit.CollectionDefinitionAttribute.DisableParallelization.html).

M1: the loaded loops exclude the repro, and with it the drain and the check after Exit. M2: the check after Exit cannot detect a stray cancel on one CPU, or on a local listing that never waits. m6: the full-suite proof is idle-only. The loaded class ×30 for the flaky test itself is sound and matches the measured baseline.

none beyond correctness: in-process, THREAD_TERMINATE on the process's own threads, no elevation. The one abuse-shaped risk, a cancel landing on a reused thread handle that belongs to another worker, is covered under M4 and m2.
